> **What this case shows** — a photoplethysmogram (**PPG** — the optical pulse a
> smartwatch or pulse-oximeter measures) and an ECG record the same heartbeat two
> different ways. On 52 ICU recordings the ecosystem's **PPG pulse rate** tracks
> the simultaneous **ECG heart rate** closely: **r = 0.96**, mean bias **−2.1 bpm**,
> 95% limits of agreement **[−9.4, +5.1] bpm**, and **90 %** of records within
> **±5 bpm**. **What reproduces, and what doesn't** — the agreement reproduces and
> clears the clinical heart-rate-accuracy bar; where it widens is on poorer-quality
> recordings, and one record is an **ECG-detection failure** (the *reference*
> failed, not the PPG) — flagged and set aside, not hidden. **How to read it** —
> left, each record's PPG rate against its ECG rate on the identity line; right, the
> Bland–Altman plot showing the bias and the limits of agreement.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — validate one sensor against a reference in three moves: **detect**
the events in each signal → **reduce** each to the same summary (a rate) →
**agree** with a Bland–Altman method comparison, not just a correlation.
**Way of thinking** — a correlation only says the two move together; *agreement*
(bias + limits) says whether one can stand in for the other. Judge the *reference*
too — an implausible reference value is a detection failure to exclude on an
objective rule, not a data point to average in.
**Ecosystem usage** — the same `PhysioExperiment` carries both channels, so PPG
and ECG go through parallel one-function-per-role chains
(`readWFDB` → `ppgDetectPulses`/`pulseRateVariability`; `readWFDB` →
`ecgDetectRpeaks` → `ecgRRintervals`). The final section makes this reusable.
:::

## Proposition

Across 52 ICU recordings the PPG-derived pulse rate agrees with the simultaneous
ECG heart rate: **Pearson r 0.96**, Bland–Altman **bias −2.1 bpm** with **95%
limits of agreement [−9.4, +5.1] bpm**, mean absolute error **2.2 bpm**, and
**90 %** of records within **±5 bpm**.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from what the dataset pairs together.** BIDMC provides
**simultaneous** photoplethysmogram (PLETH) and ECG from ICU patient monitors —
assembled to benchmark vital-sign algorithms (Pimentel et al., 2017). The optical
PPG is the signal a wrist wearable or a fingertip pulse-oximeter actually sees;
the ECG is the electrical gold standard. So we ask the foundational
wearable-monitoring question the paired channels let us answer directly: **does
the optical pulse recover the electrical heartbeat** — closely enough that a PPG
pulse rate can stand in for an ECG heart rate?

## Challenge & approach

Two different measurements of "the same" quantity never match exactly, and a
correlation hides that: it can be high while one device reads systematically fast
or drifts far on some records. The right tool is a **Bland–Altman** method
comparison — the bias (mean difference) and the limits of agreement (how far apart
they can be). We detect the beats in each signal, reduce each record to a mean
rate, and compare:

```
readWFDB → PLETH → ppgDetectPulses / pulseRateVariability   (PPG pulse rate)
readWFDB → II    → ecgDetectRpeaks → ecgRRintervals          (ECG heart rate)
```

The ECG rate is the reference — so we also **judge the reference**: a record whose
ECG rate is physiologically implausible (here one record at 30 bpm, from an R-peak
detection failure) is excluded on an **objective** rule (ECG rate outside
40–180 bpm), not because it disagrees with the PPG.

## Data

**BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset** (PhysioNet) — public
(<https://physionet.org/content/bidmc/1.0.0/>), ODbL. 53 eight-minute ICU
recordings with **PLETH (PPG)** and **II (ECG)** at 125 Hz. The exact records
(with checksums) are in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json). *Pimentel MAF, et
al. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 2017;64(8):1914–23; Goldberger AL, et al. Circulation.
2000;101(23):e215–20.*

## Results

![Left: each record's PPG pulse rate against its ECG heart rate; the points hug the identity line (r = 0.96), and the one excluded ECG-detection failure is marked. Right: the Bland–Altman plot — the difference (PPG − ECG) against the mean rate, with the −2.1 bpm bias and the [−9.4, +5.1] bpm limits of agreement.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* on the left, closeness to the dashed identity line is
agreement; on the right, the solid line is the average offset (bias) and the
dashed lines are the range within which 95 % of differences fall.

**Agreement** ([`artifacts/ppg_ecg_agreement.csv`](artifacts/ppg_ecg_agreement.csv)),
over the **52** records with a valid ECG reference:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Pearson correlation | **0.96** |
| Mean bias (PPG − ECG) | **−2.1 bpm** |
| 95% limits of agreement | **[−9.4, +5.1] bpm** |
| Mean absolute error | **2.2 bpm** |
| Within ±5 bpm / ±10 bpm | **90.4 % / 96.2 %** |

This clears the ANSI/AAMI EC13 heart-rate-accuracy bar (±5 bpm or ±10 %). One of
the 53 records (**bidmc03**) was excluded as an **ECG-reference detection failure**
— its R-peak detector found only 225 beats, an implausible 30 bpm — flagged by the
objective ECG-rate rule, not by its disagreement with the PPG
([`artifacts/ppg_ecg_per_record.csv`](artifacts/ppg_ecg_per_record.csv)). The
widest surviving differences are on records with poorer signal quality (ICU motion
or arrhythmia), where PPG–ECG agreement loosens — shown in full.

## Conclusion

On public ICU monitoring the ecosystem's optical PPG pulse rate stands in for the
ECG heart rate to clinical accuracy, quantified honestly with a Bland–Altman
agreement rather than a bare correlation. The transferable lesson is to validate a
sensor by **agreement, not correlation**, and to **judge the reference** — an
implausible gold-standard value is a detection failure to exclude on a rule, not a
disagreement to average away.

## Open questions

Agreement here is a per-record mean pulse rate vs mean heart rate. Beat-to-beat
pulse-rate-variability tracking — and how it degrades under motion, arrhythmia, or
poor perfusion — is a finer question the paired signals support but this case does
not pursue. Documented, not escalated.

## Using this in your own analysis

This case is a worked example of a **cross-modal agreement study** — the pattern
for "can sensor A stand in for reference B?" for any paired measurement.

**The general recipe** (three steps):

1. **Detect** the events in each signal — PPG systolic pulses and ECG R-peaks.
2. **Reduce** each record to the *same* summary on the *same* window — here a mean
   rate in bpm.
3. **Agree** with Bland–Altman: report the bias and the 95% limits of agreement
   (and % within a clinical tolerance), and screen the reference for failures.

**Which functions, and how they compose.** Each step is one ecosystem function,
picked by *role* — I/O → analysis — and both modalities share the data model:

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| load the paired PPG + ECG record | `readWFDB()` | PhysioIO |
| detect PPG systolic pulses | `ppgDetectPulses()` | PhysioECG |
| PPG pulse rate (+ variability) | `pulseRateVariability()` | PhysioECG |
| detect ECG R-peaks | `ecgDetectRpeaks()` | PhysioECG |
| ECG RR intervals → heart rate | `ecgRRintervals()` | PhysioECG |

They chain because every step consumes or returns a `PhysioExperiment` — one
channel of the same object becomes the PPG chain, another the ECG chain, so you
compare two modalities without leaving the data model.

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **Channel selection** — pick the PPG (`PLETH`) and a clean ECG lead (`II`) by
  name from the record's channels.
- **PPG band-pass (`low`, `high`) / `refractory_ms`** in `ppgDetectPulses()` — keep
  the pulse band (~0.5–8 Hz) and set the refractory period below the shortest
  plausible beat interval; widen for noisy wrist PPG.
- **Analysis window** — reduce both signals over the *same* interval so the two
  rates are comparable; screen the reference (implausible ECG rate ⇒ exclude).

**Applying it to your own hypothesis.** Swap in your own paired signals (wrist PPG
vs chest ECG, a new HR algorithm vs a reference), keep the detect → rate →
Bland–Altman recipe, and report agreement plus the reference-failure screen. The
ECG half of this recipe is exactly the heart-rate and HRV pipeline used on MIT-BIH
and Fantasia ([`ecg-hr-spectrum-mitbih`](../ecg-hr-spectrum-mitbih/),
[`ecg-hrv-aging-fantasia`](../ecg-hrv-aging-fantasia/)).

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioIO); library(PhysioECG)

rates <- function(rec) {
  pe  <- readWFDB(rec)                                          # PLETH + II @ 125 Hz
  lab <- toupper(SummarizedExperiment::colData(pe)$label)
  ppg <- pulseRateVariability(pe[, which(grepl("PLETH", lab))[1]])$time$mean_pr
  peE <- pe[, which(grepl("II", lab))[1]]
  rr  <- ecgRRintervals(peE, ecgDetectRpeaks(peE, method = "pan_tompkins"))
  c(ppg = ppg, ecg = 60000 / mean(rr$rr_ms))                   # PPG vs ECG rate, bpm
}

r <- rates("bidmc01"); r["ppg"] - r["ecg"]                     # per-record difference
```

**Auditing the numbers.** For readers who want to verify rather than trust: every
record's PPG and ECG rate, the agreement statistics, and the reference-failure
flag live in [`artifacts/`](artifacts/), and `audit.py` re-derives the bias, the
limits of agreement, the MAE, and the ±5 bpm fraction — and re-checks the objective
exclusion — from those files.
